title: Office of Kaiju Affairs WebMCP
pitch: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing.
about_excerpt: The Office of Kaiju Affairs turns a 51-page simulated government site into seven citable, constraint-aware WebMCP tools at publish time, then publicly benchmarks them against ordinary agent browsing. Like Comment Story Updates Office of Kaiju Affairs Swap the kaiju for the DMV. We built a 51-page government site whose CMS automatically turns published content into WebMCP tools—then ran 95 recorded trials to find out when those tools actually help. Live site: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/ The Arena: https://office-of-kaiju-affairs.vercel.app/arena/ Source code: https://github.com/heitham/Office-of-Kaiju-Affairs Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ksu90tndo5U Inspiration The kaiju left. The paperwork did not. Mira Tanaka’s bakery has been damaged. She needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer about what she owes. Unfortunately, she now faces something almost as intimidating as a kaiju: a government website. Government websites are where ordinary people meet extraordinary complexity, sometimes at the worst of times: eligibility rules, buried exceptions, long document lists, and forms with real consequences. Agents can already navigate these sites—but today they usually do it by reading pages, following links, and guessing which sentence or field matters. We wanted to explore a more ambitious question than “can an agent call a tool?” What if a large website could publish an agent interface as naturally as it publishes a page—and prove whether that interface is worth using? The Office of Kaiju Affairs is our fictional test case: a national agency handling kaiju-attack damage claims, post-attack reconstruction permits, evacuation routes, and public information. What it does The project has three connected parts. 1. A complete public-service website The Office is a working, 51-page government-style site published by RIFT , my headless CMS. Citizens can browse services, understand policy, locate an office, check claim requirements, and complete a proximity-construction permit. 2. An agent layer generated by the CMS At publish time, the CMS emits a manifest describing the rendered site: pages, summaries, key facts, services, eligibility rules, citations, offices, and form schemas. A small browser runtime turns that manifest into seven WebMCP tools: search_site — finds facts across the entire published site get_page_summary — reads a page as structured, citable data list_services — explains what the agency offers get_service_requirements — returns documents, fees, deadlines, and fields check_eligibility — evaluates a citizen's facts against published rules prefill_permit_form — validates and fills the visible form, but cannot submit it get_office_info — finds offices and evacuation routes This is the important architectural idea: we did not hand-code one tool per page. Content becomes capability at publish time. Add or update a CMS page, republish, and the agent interface changes with the website. The manifest is intentionally lightweight. It does not pretend to be a government's single source of truth. It gives agents a navigable map of what this publisher knows: the services, sources, rules, forms, and capabilities represented on this part of the public web. RIFT itself predates this challenge and remains proprietary. For the challenge, I used RIFT to publish the fictional Office of Kaiju Affairs site with WebMCP publishing integration. The published website, the open-source browser runtime, all seven tools, the Arena, the task design, the answer keys, and the evaluation pipeline are the submission. The public repository contains every component needed to run and inspect the WebMCP project; it does not contain RIFT's private CMS source. 3. The Arena: a public evidence layer We looked at this as an experiment: would WebMCP be faster, safer, or more accurate? The Arena publishes 95 recorded runs of the same three citizen tasks across: a UI lane, where the agent reads pages and navigates without WebMCP; a WebMCP lane, where the agent uses the site's registered tools; two model tiers, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5; and two rounds, before and after fixes discovered by the benchmark. Every score, timing, action count, and range is computed from the trace files at runtime. The traces, answer keys, tool arguments, elapsed milliseconds, and earlier results are all public. Judges can also copy each scenario and run the WebMCP lane themselves. The recorded benchmark uses two Claude model tiers to test how the same interface behaves as model capability changes. The Arena is deliberately model-independent: in ChatGPT's WebMCP-enabled browser, the judge's OpenAI agent becomes the live lane and can attempt the same published tasks against the same answer keys. Three citizen experiences Find the rule—not just an answer Mira Tanaka is filing a second damage claim. The obvious reading says she qualifies for a fee waiver; the actual rule says only approved claims count, so her pending claim does not. The agent must find the buried exception, explain that the ¥12,000 fee is still payable, and point Mira to the source. WebMCP makes the site's search index and rule citations directly available instead of forcing the agent to infer structure from navigation. Turn policy into a complete checklist Mira's eligibility depends on several rules spread across multiple pages: her zone, structural damage, income, business status, insurance payout, claims history, and filing window. check_eligibility evaluates those facts against a ruleset published as data. It returns the outcome, three applicable grants, five required documents, and citations. In our recorded results, both model tiers scored 100% in both lanes—but WebMCP reached the result with fewer actions and was 1.7× faster for Sonnet and 2.1× faster for Haiku . Fill the form, then hand control back For a proximity-construction permit, the agent must derive the K-2 reinforcement standard from Mira's Zone 4 location, validate twelve values against the published schema, and fill the real form. Then it must stop. prefill_permit_form has no submission capability. It fills and highlights the fields, reports what it entered or rejected, and leaves the final action to the person. The safety boundary is structural, not a hopeful instruction in a prompt. What our experiment found The most useful result was not “tools always win.” They did not. On this small, well-structured site, the stronger model often navigated the UI successfully. In the headline Sonnet runs, 14 of 15 UI-lane passes received full marks. Across all three Sonnet tasks, WebMCP also used about 2.4× as many context tokens on average—19,422 versus 8,117—because tool schemas and responses add context to the model's calls. That cost was not uniform: on the eligibility task, where the tool performed the most substantive rule evaluation, WebMCP used fewer tokens than browsing for both model sizes. video_transcript_excerpt: Mira Tanaka survived a Kaiju attack. Now she needs compensation, a rebuilding permit, and a straight answer from the government. Unfortunately, her best help is a website and an AI agent trying to understand it. Government websites contain real decisions hidden across policy pages, exceptions, document lists, and forms. AI agents can help ease the stress, but they must reconstruct the service from site navigation and text. We built a complete 51-page fictional government agency enabled with Web MCP. When the CMS publishes the website, it also generates a machine-readable manifest. A small browser runtime converts that content into seven Web MCP tools for search, services, eligibility, requirements, offices, and forms. Mira's eligibility depends on her location, damage, income, insurance, business status, and filing window. An AI agent would need to browse the website and find that through brute-force web browsing. With Web MCP check eligibility, evaluate the publisher's encoded rules, and return the outcome: three applicable grants, five required documents, and supporting citations. We built tests to see if Web MCP could outperform an agent browsing the website directly. You can use your ChatGPT Web MCP browser to help Mira submit her construction permit form online. For the permit, Web MCP validates 12 values, derives the required reinforcement standard, and fills the real form. Then it stops. The tool exposes no submission operation. Mira reviews the highlighted fields and makes the final decision herself. Human control is part of the capability. We did not stop at a polished demo. The arena publishes 95 inspectable runs comparing Web MCP with ordinary browsing across three tasks, two model sizes, and two rounds. Web MCP was not always better, but it completed the eligibility task with fewer actions and substantially less time, and it reduced the accuracy loss when we moved to the smaller model. Our most important finding was not about speed. When policy becomes executable, meaning can be lost between the approved sentence and the encoded rule. A citation may point to the correct page while the logic still misses an exception. Agent native publishing therefore creates a new responsibility. Organizations must review not only what people will read, but what machines will execute. The Office of Kaiju Affairs is fictional. The civic problem is not. WebMCP gives public institutions a way to participate in the agent experience instead of leaving every agent to reverse engineer their websites. And the open source arena we shared gives citizens, publishers, and judges a way to measure where WebMCP helps.

live_observation.first_impression: A polished simulated government homepage lists services for kaiju damage, permits, evacuation, offices, and developer docs.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked the Kaiju Damage Compensation service card.
live_observation.after_state: The page remained on the same homepage after the click; no service detail or visible transition appeared.
live_observation.notes: The public site was reachable and its purpose was clear, but the primary service link did not visibly respond in this session.
